items.front: Who appoints the RBI Governor and from where do the Governor's powers flow?
items.back: Appointed by the Central Government; powers flow from the RBI Act, 1934 (not the Constitution). RBI Act 1934; began ops 1 Apr 1935; nationalised 1949.

items.front: MPC — how many members, who chairs, casting vote?
items.back: 6 members (3 RBI incl. Governor as chair + 3 Govt-appointed experts); Governor has the casting vote; meets ≥4 times/year. NOT chaired by the FM; NOT 12-member.

items.front: Order the LAF corridor: SDF, Repo, MSF/Bank Rate.
items.back: SDF (floor) < Repo < MSF = Bank Rate (ceiling). SDF (2022) absorbs liquidity without collateral; MSF is penal borrowing above repo.

items.front: CRR vs SLR — where is each held?
items.back: CRR = cash held WITH the RBI (earns no interest); SLR = liquid assets (cash/gold/G-secs) held by the BANK itself. Cutting SLR lets banks lend more/cut lending rates.
items.examPoint: Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) & Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR)

items.front: What is 'sterilisation' and which tool performs it?
items.back: Neutralising liquidity from forex inflows via Open Market Operations (sell G-secs); MSS (2004) is the dedicated instrument. OMO = purchase/sale of G-secs by RBI.
items.examPoint: Open Market Operations (OMO) & Market Stabilisation Scheme (MSS)

items.front: The money multiplier rises with… and falls with…?
items.back: Rises with the public's banking habit (lower currency-to-deposit ratio); falls with higher CRR/SLR or cash leakage. Multiplier = 1 ÷ reserve ratio (RR 20% → 5).

items.front: Money market vs capital market — sort: call money, T-bills, G-sec bonds, stocks.
items.back: Money market (≤1 yr): call money, T-bills, CP (unsecured promissory note), CD. Capital market (long-term): G-sec/bond market, stock market.
items.examPoint: Financial markets — money vs capital, primary vs secondary & SEBI

items.front: What is MCLR and why was it introduced (2016)?
items.back: Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate — RBI benchmark for bank lending; for transparency & quicker rate-cut transmission (replaced base rate). Now supplemented by external benchmark (EBLR).

items.front: Payments banks — can they lend or issue credit cards?
items.back: No lending, no credit cards; debit cards only; deposits ≤₹2 lakh (RBI 2014, Nachiket Mor Cmte). Small Finance Banks CAN lend (75% PSL) to small units/marginal farmers.
items.examPoint: Payments banks — RBI 2014 guidelines, ₹2 lakh deposit cap, no lending/credit cards

items.front: Inflation target and who compiles CPI/WPI?
items.back: CPI target 4% ±2% (2–6%), reviewed every 5 yrs; RBI targets CPI (compiled by NSO). WPI by Office of Economic Adviser (DPIIT); core inflation excludes food & fuel.
NPCI (2008), promoted by RBI & IBA under PSS Act 2007; runs RuPay (2012), IMPS (2010), UPI (2016), BBPS. UPI accepted in UAE, France, Singapore (PayNow), Bhutan, Nepal, Sri Lanka, Mauritius.
items.examPoint: NPCI — umbrella retail-payments organisation (2008, RBI/IBA, PSS Act 2007)

items.back: RTGS = real-time, large-value ≥₹2 lakh, 24×7 (RBI); NEFT = batch, no minimum, 24×7 (RBI). IMPS & UPI are NPCI systems. Digital Rupee (CBDC) pilots began 2022.
items.examPoint: IMPS, NEFT & RTGS — RBI/NPCI fund-transfer systems (24x7; RTGS large-value ≥₹2 lakh)

items.front: Basel III / CAR and who regulates credit-rating agencies?
items.back: Basel III improves banks' ability to absorb stress; CAR (CRAR) min 9% in India (Basel 8%). Credit-rating agencies (CRISIL, ICRA, CARE) are regulated by SEBI, not RBI. PSL = 40% of ANBC.
